unit.title: Analysing a market
unit.description: SWOT, PESTEL, Porter five forces, BCG matrix, Ansoff matrix, product life cycle, market share

cards.definition: A model to judge how attractive an industry is: rivalry between competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers and bargaining power of suppliers.
cards.example: Food delivery apps face strong rivalry, restaurants with growing power and customers who switch for 2 euros: low profits.

cards.definition: A portfolio grid crossing market growth and relative market share: Stars (high, high), Cash cows (low growth, high share), Question marks (high growth, low share) and Dogs (low, low).
cards.example: A cash cow product funds the marketing of a question mark that might become a star.

cards.definition: Four growth paths: market penetration (existing product, existing market), product development (new product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market) and diversification (new product, new market, the riskiest).
cards.example: A French meal kit brand launching in Belgium is market development.

cards.definition: The stages a product category goes through: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Marketing priorities change at each stage, from education to differentiation to cost control.
cards.example: Streaming video is mature in France: growth slows and services fight on price and exclusive content.

cards.definition: A SWOT is only useful when crossed: use strengths to seize opportunities, fix weaknesses that threats would exploit. A list of 40 bullets nobody acts on is not analysis.
cards.example: Strength: a loyal community. Opportunity: a rising trend for repair. Action: launch a repair service promoted by the community.

exercises.prompt: In a SWOT, which items are internal to the company?
exercises.explain: Strengths and weaknesses are inside (team, product, budget). Opportunities and threats come from the outside (market, law, competitors).

exercises.prompt: A new EU law restricts the use of personal data for ads. In a PESTEL, where does it go?
exercises.explain: PESTEL: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal. A new regulation is Legal; a government policy change would be Political.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of Porter five forces?
choices: The size of your marketing budget
exercises.explain: The five forces describe the industry, not your own resources: rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers and suppliers.

exercises.prompt: For a cinema, video streaming at home is which force?
exercises.explain: A substitute meets the same need in a different way. Another cinema would be a rival; streaming is a substitute.

exercises.prompt: In the BCG matrix, what is a product with low market growth but a high relative share?
exercises.explain: Cash cows dominate a mature market: they need little investment and generate cash that funds stars and question marks.

exercises.prompt: A sneaker brand starts selling the same sneakers in Japan. Which Ansoff quadrant?
exercises.explain: Existing product, new market: market development. Diversification would be a new product in a new market, the riskiest move.

exercises.prompt: A bank launches its own phone plans for new customers. Which Ansoff quadrant?
exercises.explain: New product and new market at once: diversification. It can work, but it uses few of the existing strengths.

exercises.prompt: A category is in maturity: sales plateau and everyone knows the product. What usually becomes the priority?
choices: Explaining what the product is used for
Opening many distributors as fast as possible
Stopping all communication to save money
exercises.explain: In maturity growth comes from stealing share or keeping customers. Education was the priority at introduction.

exercises.prompt: A long SWOT with 40 bullets is a better analysis than a short one with 8.
exercises.explain: False. The value is in crossing the four boxes and deciding. A short SWOT that leads to three clear actions beats an exhaustive list.

exercises.prompt: Your brand sells 2 million euros in a 10 million euro market. What is your market share in value?
exercises.explain: 2 divided by 10. Market share can be measured in value (euros) or in volume (units); always say which one.

exercises.title: Should we enter this market?
exercises.scenario: Your organic baby food brand sells in French supermarkets. The board wants to launch an organic pet food range sold in pet shops.

steps.prompt: Which Ansoff quadrant is this move?
choices: Market penetration: more of the same
Product development: new product, same buyers
steps.feedback: Pet food is a new product, sold to pet owners through pet shops: a new market. It is the riskiest quadrant.

steps.prompt: A Porter analysis shows three giants own 80 percent of pet food and pet shops ask for big margins. Which forces are strong?
choices: Rivalry and the power of distributors
steps.feedback: Powerful incumbents and demanding retailers squeeze newcomers. Your strength (organic baby food know-how) helps little against them.

steps.prompt: What do you recommend to the board?
choices: First test a small range online to measure demand
Launch 40 products in all pet shops at once
Drop baby food to fund the new range
Copy the price and packs of the market leader
steps.feedback: A cheap test reduces the risk of a diversification. The decision comes after data, not before.

exercises.explain: Name the move, weigh the market forces, then reduce risk with a test before committing.
